title: Quantum Entanglement
hook: Two particles can share one quantum state so tightly that measuring one instantly fixes the other's matching property — even light-years apart. Einstein called it spooky.
key_points: Entangled particles share a single quantum state, so their properties are linked.
Measuring one instantly determines the matching property of the other, at any distance.
Experiments have confirmed it — Einstein's 'spooky action at a distance' is real.
It cannot send messages faster than light: each outcome on its own is random.
content_html: In quantum mechanics, two particles can become entangled — woven into a single shared quantum state. Once that happens, their properties are correlated: measure one and you instantly learn the matching property of the other, even if the two have since drifted light-years apart. Einstein found this so unsettling that he called it "spooky action at a distance" and doubted it could be the whole story.
extra_html: Decades of increasingly careful experiments have confirmed that the correlations are real and genuinely defy any tidy local explanation. But there's a crucial limit that's easy to get wrong: entanglement cannot be used to send a message faster than light. Each individual measurement gives a random result that you can't control, so there's no way to encode information in it — the trick only becomes visible when both parties later compare notes through ordinary channels. The same correlations are a key resource in quantum computing and quantum cryptography. Wikipedia covers the experiments and the no-faster-than-light caveat in detail.

related.title: What Makes Quantum Physics Weird
related.hook: In the quantum world energy comes in lumps, particles act like waves, and you can't pin down everything at once — and yet it's our best-tested theory.

related.title: Is Light a Wave or a Particle?
related.hook: Light behaves like a wave in some experiments and like a stream of particles in others — and the surprising answer is that it's both.

related.title: Qubits and Quantum Computing
related.hook: A normal bit is a 0 or a 1. A qubit can be both at once — and linking many of them lets a quantum computer explore a staggering number of possibilities together.

related.title: A Schrödinger's Cat Built From Quantum Parts
related.hook: Cat states usually superpose two near-classical blobs of motion. Oxford built one from purely quantum ingredients — and could sculpt the superposition into almost any shape.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean for two particles to be entangled?
flashcards.back_html: They share a single quantum state, so measuring one instantly determines the matching property of the other, no matter how far apart they are.

flashcards.prompt: Can entanglement be used to send messages faster than light?

choices.text: No — each measurement outcome on its own is random
Yes — the link is instant, so it carries information instantly
Only if the particles are very close together

flashcards.explanation_html: Although the correlation is instant, you can't control your own random outcome, so no usable information travels faster than light.

flashcards.prompt: What did Einstein famously call entanglement?
flashcards.explanation_html: Einstein was deeply uneasy with entanglement and dubbed it 'spooky action at a distance'; later experiments confirmed the effect is real.
